info.bio:
Bob Dylan nació con el nombre de Robert Allen Zimmerman el 24 de mayo de 1941 en Duluth, Minnesota (Estados Unidos). Está considerado uno de los compositores y músicos más influyentes y prolíficos del siglo XX y ha sido nominado varias veces al Premio Nobel de Literatura. 
En 2007 fue galardonado con el Premio Príncipe de Asturias de las Artes por ser un "mito viviente" de la historia de la música popular y "faro de una generación que tuvo el sueño de cambiar el mundo".

scenes.name: Bob Dylan y el rock eléctrico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Una «presencia encapuchada» en todo el libro aunque no se le dedica un capítulo. Robert Shelton, crítico del New York Times que en 1961 le escribió la primera reseña favorable y lo lanzó, lo pone a la cabeza de los poetas-músicos que llevaban el pop a la realidad sin barnizar en su ensayo «Orpheus Plugs In» para la revista Aspen: la fusión de música, poesía, baile, luces y cine era «una nueva forma de arte total». En marzo de 1966 Shelton lo entrevistó en un avión entre Nebraska y Colorado. Para sentir 1966 en crudo, dice Savage, basta escuchar cualquiera de sus conciertos acústicos de abril y mayo.

scenes.name: Contracultura, Sgt. Pepper y Woodstock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.

scenes.name: Folk revival y canción protesta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El acontecimiento más importante del cambio de década: el folk revival (Kingston Trio, festival de Newport) convierte la música en algo más que entretenimiento. Con «Blowing In The Wind» de Dylan, la canción protesta se vuelve el paradigma del Greenwich Village y el folk-singer muta en cantautor. Otros buscan la innovación: Davy Graham, Sandy Bull (fusión de folk, blues, jazz y raga) y John Fahey, que inventa el «American primitivism».

scenes.name: Contracultura: cantautores eléctricos
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La fusión de música y política convierte el rock en vehículo de la disidencia: la contracultura. Todo empieza con Bob Dylan, el músico más influyente de los sesenta, que redefine el rock como composición metafísica y libre (Highway 61 Revisited, Blonde On Blonde). La transición del folk-singer al cantautor eléctrico abre infinitas vías: Fred Neil, Tim Hardin, Neil Diamond, Paul Simon (el poeta del chico tímido y solitario), Donovan (la quintaesencia del ideal hippy) y Country Joe McDonald, agit-prop de Berkeley.

scenes.name: Folk-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Más invento de productores (Tom Wilson, Terry Melcher) que movimiento artístico: el espíritu del Mersey-beat en clave americana. Byrds y Beau Brummels crean el «jingle-jangle»; los Byrds encadenan folk-rock, acid-rock, raga-rock («Eight Miles High») y country-rock (Sweetheart Of The Rodeo). Mamas & Papas, Turtles, Lovin' Spoonful, Buffalo Springfield y, sobre todo, Tim Buckley, que funde folk, blues, jazz, psicodelia y música de cámara y convierte la voz en un instrumento (Happy Sad, Lorca, Starsailor).

scenes.name: Psicodelia y acid-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: En 1965 San Francisco se convierte en la ciudad más efervescente del país: los Grateful Dead tocan en los «acid tests» de Ken Kesey, nace la escena hippy y en 1966-67 llega el verano del amor. El acid-rock, evolución del folk-rock pensada como banda sonora del viaje de LSD, es el equivalente rockero de la pintura abstracta, el free jazz y la poesía beat: su gran invento es la «jam», con la guitarra eléctrica al mando y un espíritu zen en lugar del dolor del blues. Jefferson Airplane encarnan la era; los Grateful Dead inventan la improvisación colectiva libre (Anthem Of The Sun, Live Dead); Kaleidoscope, Moby Grape, Quicksilver, Blue Cheer o Fifty Foot Hose amplían el abanico. Monterey y Sgt Pepper (1967) convierten lo alternativo en mainstream. Fuera de California, Jimi Hendrix declara la guerra a la armonía occidental con su guitarra.

scenes.name: Blues revival y blues-rock
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: John Mayall define con Bluesbreakers (con Eric Clapton) el rhythm'n'blues tocado por blancos europeos, el blues-rock, y siembra el progresivo con sus discos de jazz y lounge. Su equivalente americano es Al Kooper (Blues Project, Supersession, Blood Sweat & Tears). Cream, el primer power-trio, cambia la cara del rock británico con improvisación de jazz, distorsión y solos interminables; Fleetwood Mac de Peter Green y Ten Years After llevan del blues al hard rock. En San Francisco, Janis Joplin, Steve Miller y Santana; en Los Ángeles, Taj Mahal y Ry Cooder reconstruyen las tradiciones; Bob Seger casa el grito soul con el Detroit obrero.

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

scenes.name: Alt-country
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La revolución iniciada en Chicago por Souled American y Uncle Tupelo (No Depression: baladas country con la furia del hardcore) se convierte en los noventa en un género propio: sus herederos abandonan el hardcore por los sonidos más espartanos y tradicionales. Son Volt de Jay Farrar y Wilco de Jeff Tweedy (Being There, Yankee Hotel Foxtrot); Will Oldham (Palace) arranca el movimiento; Freakwater, Ida, Handsome Family, Retsin, Blue Mountain, Whiskeytown, Grant Lee Buffalo, Citizens' Utilities, Willard Grant Conspiracy. El «chamber folk» de Lambchop, Lullaby For The Working Class, Geraldine Fibbers y Pinetop Seven; el country-rock de Volebeats, Ass Ponys, Sixteen Horsepower, Old 97's y los terroristas Grifters; el folk-rock de Swell, Counting Crows, Cracker, Cake, Hootie & The Blowfish; los Black Crowes; Belle And Sebastian, Arab Strap y los polacos Atman.

scenes.name: Slo-core
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Una de las innovaciones más importantes de los noventa: versión lenta, onírica y melancólica del dream-pop, descendiente de Galaxie 500 y Yo La Tengo, con composiciones largas y contenidas. Codeine la consagran (Frigid Stars); Seam, Red House Painters de Mark Kozelek (Down Colorful Hill), Low (I Could Live In Hope, Trust: el haiku del rock) y Bedhead. La balada etérea femenina: Mazzy Star, His Name Is Alive, Moon Seven Times, Congo Norvell, Helium, Elysian Fields. La balada atmosférica: Idaho, Acetone, Low Road, American Analog Set, Calla, y el «rock textural» del Noroeste: Built To Spill (Perfect From Now On), Silkworm, Red Stars Theory, Death Cab For Cutie. En Inglaterra, Drugstore, Mojave 3, Movietone.

podcast.title: Discovered by John Hammond (1960)
podcast.body: Bob Dylan was discovered and signed by legendary talent scout John Hammond in 1960, the same year Hammond signed Aretha Franklin. Dylan, originally from Duluth, Minnesota, was brought into the Columbia Records fold as Hammond was especially busy at the start of the 1960s. "In a year of signing Detroit native Aretha Franklin, he discovered and signed a young man from Duluth, Minnesota, who went by Bob Dylan."

podcast.title: Meeting Woody Guthrie (1961)
podcast.body: In January 1961, Dylan moved to New York with the goal of meeting Woody Guthrie, who was severely ill with Huntington's disease and hospitalized. Dylan visited Guthrie regularly, playing his own songs for him and occasionally joining family visits. These months of interaction deeply affected Dylan. "In January 1961, he decided he was going to go to New York, and while he was there, he was going to go and meet Woody Guthrie in person."

podcast.title: Embracing Electric Guitar (1965)
podcast.body: Bob Dylan's decision to start using an electric guitar in 1965 marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of popular music, signaling a new phase where the electric guitar became even more central to musical expression. This shift had a profound impact on the direction of folk and rock music. "And when Bob Dylan started using an electric guitar in 1965, we entered a whole new phase of evolution."

podcast.title: Shift Towards Album as Artistic Statement (Circa 1965)
podcast.body: Around 1965, prominent artists such as The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and The Beach Boys began to pivot from focusing on individual singles towards conceptualizing albums as complete artistic statements, typically comprising ten, twelve, or more interconnected tracks. "But starting in around 1965, a number of artists, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, and the Beach Boys among them, began to think less in terms of individual songs."

podcast.title: Shifting Album Perception (c. 1965)
podcast.body: Around 1965, Bob Dylan, along with The Beatles, recognized the album's potential as a cohesive artistic work, which prompted a shift towards writing longer, more complex songs and sequenced collections rather than simply releasing singles. "The Beatles, Bob Dylan, and a few others looked at the album and thought, I can work with this."

podcast.title: Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction (1982)
podcast.body: Bob Dylan was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1982, and notably, the only person he would allow to be photographed with him at the event was Dina Shore. "in 1982 Bob Dylan was inducted into the song writers Hall of Fame and the only person that he would have his photo. podcast.title: Controversial Live Aid Remark
podcast.body: During his performance at Live Aid in Philadelphia on July 13, 1985, which was arguably "one of the worst performances of his life," Bob Dylan, alongside Keith Richards and Ron Wood of The Rolling Stones, made a somewhat offhanded remark. He suggested that it would be beneficial if some of the money raised to fight famine in Ethiopia could also be used to help American farmers pay their mortgages. This comment drew criticism, including from Bob Geldof, who felt it diverted attention from the primary cause. "Not everyone was happy with that remark including Bob Gildoff who seemed to think it was kind of drawing attention away from the cause at hand maybe but it also did get the attention of Willie Nelson a Texan who was well aware of the plight of the American farmers and said he had been thinking about doing some type of benefit for them for a couple of years."

podcast.title: Robert Johnson Influence
podcast.body: John Hammond gave Dylan a copy of Robert Johnson's "King of the Delta Blues Singers" before its public release. xref.title: Family Background and Early Influences
xref.body: Born in 1969, Jacob Dylan is the son of Bob Dylan and his model wife Sarah Dylan, who were married secretly in November 1965. Sarah inspired lyrics for many of Bob Dylan's songs before their 1977 divorce. Despite his father being a famous folk singer, Jacob preferred punk bands like The Clash, The Buzzcocks, and The Jam in his youth, and later had an aborted attempt at design school in New York. "Jacob Dylan is the son of Bob and his model wife Sarah Dylan. They were married in secret in November 1965. And for the next dozen years, she inspired the lyrics for a number of Dylan songs. Then they divorced in 1977. But before then, Jacob came along. That was 1969. xref.title: John Wayne Gacy's Musical Preference
xref.body: Serial killer John Wayne Gacy, who claimed at least 33 victims, was known to be an admirer of REO Speedwagon, among other musical acts. This information offers a glimpse into his personal tastes. "John Wayne Gacy... was into Elton John, Bob Dylan, Neil Diamond, and Aureo Speedwagon."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kingston Upbringing and Early Influences
xref.body: Grew up in Kingston, sharing high school with future members of The Tragically Hip and David Usher. He struggled academically but was intensely drawn to rock and roll, absorbing music from his older siblings and becoming a huge Bob Dylan fan. "I remember being 18 and I grew up in Kingston with David Usher and the guys in the hip. We all went to the same high school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Headstones: In Their Own Words Part 1

xref.title: Learning Guitar & Songwriting (Age 20)
xref.body: At the age of 20, Matthew Good picked up a guitar for the first time. He taught himself about four or five open chords and immediately began writing his own songs, rather than learning others' material. His early compositions were simple, often using E minor C progressions with many verses, reflecting his admiration for Bob Dylan. "I picked up a guitar for the first time and I taught myself about four or five open chords and I started writing songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Matt Good: In His Own Words - Part 1

xref.title: Marcus Mumford's Musical Influences
xref.body: Growing up, Marcus Mumford was exposed to Bob Dylan's music (especially his "God Love and Era" and the *O Brother, Where Art Thou?* soundtrack) and various jazz. He played in a jazz group as a teenager. "As he grew up, Marcus was exposed to the music of Bob Dylan, especially his God Love and Era, the old brother were at the O Soundtrack, and a variety of jazz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York Underground Origins
xref.body: Unlike Bob Dylan, who came from the folk scene and secured a major record deal, Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground originated from the streets of New York City and were deemed too unconventional for mainstream consumption, especially due to their explicit subject matter. "Lou and the Velvet were from the streets of New York City and were just too weird for mainstream consumption."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nurturing Musical Environment
xref.body: The Kiszka brothers were raised in a "musically nurturing environment" that extended beyond just music to include film and literature. They were surrounded by traditional music, including early American blues artists like Elmore James, Willie Dixon, Robert Johnson, Muddy Waters, and Howlin' Wolf, as well as folk artists like Arlo Guthrie, Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell, and John Denver, primarily from their parents' vinyl collection. "we were kind of raised in a musically nurturing environment where it wasn't necessarily just music, but there was a lot of film and a lot of literature. And we had a lot of traditional music, you know, lying around."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin as The Hawks
xref.body: The Band was formed from Ronnie Hawkins's band, The Hawks, after they were "poached" by Bob Dylan. "The Hawks, who were later poached by Bob Dylan and later became The Band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

xref.title: Pioneering Albums as an Art Form
xref.body: The Beatles, alongside Bob Dylan, are credited with making music more sophisticated and releasing albums that were taken seriously, similar to jazz, classical, or Broadway recordings. This helped establish rock as a legitimate and respectable art form. "Credit can go to the Beatles and Bob Dylan because not only was their music much more sophisticated, but they also released albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pseudo-Stepdad's Record Collection
xref.body: His mother's boyfriend, Chip Donaldson, who was an English teacher and Vietnam veteran, moved in with his own record collection featuring music from the late 1960s and early 1970s, including artists like The Rolling Stones, Bob Dylan, and Grateful Dead. "It featured a lot of stuff from the late 60s and early 70s. Stones, Dylan, grateful dad, that kind of thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Ultra-Deep Background on Dave Grohl: Part 1

xref.title: Shift Towards Album-Oriented Music
xref.body: Around 1965, The Beatles, along with Bob Dylan and others, began to view the album as a creative medium, writing longer and more complex songs and carefully sequenced collections of tracks. This marked a turning point away from the singles-dominated music landscape.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Singing Style - Monotone Draw
xref.body: Starting his recording career in the late 1950s, Lou Reed's singing style deviated significantly from conventional norms. He was characterized by a limited vocal range, often speaking rather than carrying a tune, and exhibiting a monotone draw without much melody or rhythm. His timing with the music was frequently odd, a style notably different from contemporaries like Bob Dylan. "He really speaks more than he actually carries any kind of attune."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Versatile Session Musician
xref.body: Beyond Motown, Bobby Jean Hall has an impressive client list that includes a diverse range of legendary artists. Her percussion work has graced albums by Bob Dylan, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Rod Stewart, Janis Joplin, Joni Mitchell, Dolly Parton, The Doobie Brothers, Aretha Franklin, Tracy Chapman, James Taylor, and Stevie Nicks, highlighting her status as a highly sought-after session player. "Other clients have included Bob Dylan, Leonard Skinner, Rod Stewart, Janice Joplin, Joni Mitchell, Dolly Parton, The Dooby Brothers, Aretha Franklin, Tracy Chapman, James Taylor, and Stevie Nicks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

xref.title: Vocal Style and Evolution
xref.body: Leonard Cohen is described as having a unique vocal style rather than being a traditional singer who hits melodic notes. His voice is a baritone that became progressively lower and more gruff with age, often described as less musical and more of a drone or "method acting" to convey emotion. He was known to reach a low G. In the 1960s, he was initially promoted as a more musical Bob Dylan. "It's a baritone that got lower and lower and lower the older he got."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Wife and Lyric Inspiration
xref.body: Sarah Dylan, a model, married Bob Dylan in secret in November 1965. For the next dozen years, she served as the inspiration for the lyrics of many of Bob Dylan's songs. They divorced in 1977. "Sarah Dylan. They were married in secret in November 1965. And for the next dozen years, she inspired the lyrics for a number of Dylan songs. Then they divorced in 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."
